articles.title: What 220 draws actually say about hot numbers
articles.summary: We hold every Keno draw since 12 July. Widening the window from five draws to 220 collapses the gap between the hottest and coldest number from 100 points to 15 - which is randomness becoming visible.
articles.body:
Every results site publishes hot and cold numbers. Almost none of them show you the one thing that makes the data honest: what happens to the gap as you widen the window.

We hold 220 confirmed draws, from 12 July to 5 September 2026. Because 20 of 80 numbers come out each draw, every number should appear about 25% of the time over a long enough run. Here is how far the extremes sit from that baseline at each window size.

Spread between the most and least drawn number, by window size
WindowMost drawnLeast drawnSpread
5 draws100.0%0.0%100.0 pp
10 draws60.0%0.0%60.0 pp
25 draws40.0%8.0%32.0 pp
50 draws36.0%10.0%26.0 pp
100 draws35.0%15.0%20.0 pp
220 draws33.6%18.2%15.5 pp

Over the last five draws, one number appeared in every single one and several appeared in none. On a hot-and-cold widget that looks like a screaming signal. It is not. It is what five samples of a random process look like.

Stretch the same data to 220 draws and the hottest number sits at 33.6% and the coldest at 18.2% — both drifting toward 25%, exactly as they should. Nothing changed about the game. Only the sample size changed.

The numbers, for the record

Across all 220 draws, the most-drawn numbers were 41 (74 times), 66 (69) and 19 (68). The least drawn were 37 (40), 48 (41) and 56 (41). The expected count for any number is 55.

Is 74 unusually high? Not really. With 80 numbers sampled this many times, some will land well above expectation and some well below purely by chance — and which ones do it is different every time you look.

Why we still publish it

Because it is a genuine record of what happened, and because the control itself is the argument. Open our hot and cold page and move the window from 5 draws to 250. Watching the extremes converge is the clearest demonstration we can offer that short-run streaks carry no information about the next draw.

A number that has come up in 80% of the last five draws has exactly the same 25% chance next draw as one that has not appeared at all. The draw has no memory. Neither should your ticket.

articles.title: Every Keno multiplier we have recorded
articles.summary: Across 220 draws the multiplier averaged x2.03. Here is the full distribution, why it is observation rather than a published schedule, and why it never changes your odds.
articles.body:
Every NZ Keno draw carries a multiplier that scales what a winning ticket pays. Lotto NZ publish it with each result, but not, as far as we can find, the probabilities behind it. So we counted.

Across the 220 draws in our archive:

Observed Keno multiplier frequency across 220 draws
MultiplierDrawsShareRoughly
×1.511954.1%1 in 1.8
×26830.9%1 in 3.2
×3219.5%1 in 10.5
×5104.5%1 in 22
×1020.9%1 in 110

The mean works out at ×2.03. More than half of all draws carry the smallest multiplier, and ×10 showed up twice in nearly two months.

What this is not

It is not a published schedule. These are counts from a limited window, and the operator sets the real weightings. A larger sample would move these figures — treat the shape as indicative, not exact.

It is also not predictable. The multiplier on the next draw is unaffected by recent ones. A long run without a ×10 does not make one more likely, in exactly the way a long absence does not make a number due.

It does not change your odds

This is the part worth being clear about. The multiplier changes what a win pays. It has no effect whatsoever on how likely a win is. Your chance of matching numbers depends only on how many spots you play — see the full odds tables — and is identical on a ×1.5 draw and a ×10 draw.

Because it is drawn before the result and applies to everyone in that draw equally, there is also no way to select for it.

articles.title: NZ Keno draw times, confirmed across 56 days
articles.summary: Four draws a day at 10:01am, 1:01pm, 3:01pm and 6:01pm - exactly 55 draws at each time across our archive, weekends and holidays included.
articles.body:
New Zealand Keno draws four times a day. That much is widely stated. What is harder to find is confirmation that the times hold consistently — including weekends and public holidays.

Our archive covers 56 consecutive days, 12 July to 5 September 2026, and contains 220 draws. Sorted by time of day, they fall into exactly four groups:

NZ Keno draws by time of day
DrawTime (NZ)Draws recorded
Morning10:01am55
Midday1:01pm55
Afternoon3:01pm55
Evening6:01pm55

Fifty-five at each, with no gaps and no extras. Broken down by weekday the counts sit between 29 and 32 per day of the week — the variation is simply how many of each weekday fall inside a 56-day span, not a difference in schedule. Saturdays and Sundays draw the same as Tuesdays.

What it means for a limit

Four draws a day is roughly 28 a week and about 1,460 a year. Keno's odds are fixed per draw, so playing more draws does not improve them — it multiplies how often you are exposed to the same fixed house edge.

That is the practical argument for setting any limit per day or per week rather than per draw. A limit that resets four times a day is not really a limit. More on that on our responsible gambling page.

A caveat

These times are observed, not a schedule published to us. Lotto NZ set the draw calendar and can change it. If they do, this page will be out of date before we are told — the timestamp on the latest draw is always the authoritative answer to when the last one happened.
